Q: Assign names to tables in an SQL Server result set A:

I create a first (can be also last) column (an empty column only with a name)

declare @t table (c1 int, c2 varchar(10));

insert into @t values

(1, 'Line1'),(2, 'Line2'),(3, 'Line3'),(4, 'Line4'),(5, 'Line5'),(6, 'Line6'),(7, 'Line7'),(8, 'Line8'),(9, 'Line9'),(10, 'Line10');

select '' as 'EQUAL5', * from @ twhere c1 = 5;

select '' as 'LT5', * from @t where c1 < 5;

select '' as 'GT5', * from @t where c1 > 5;

Q: How to append lines from a file into new file which name bases on the content? A:

If your 75k log file is in input.txt, you can simply remove the -month-day from the first field with sub(), concatenate your output filename from that (adding "-Foo.log") and append with redirection, e.g.

awk '
  NF < 2 { next }          # skip blank line (remove if none)
  {
    yr = $1                 # save date before modifying
    sub (/-.*$/, "", yr)    # remove -month-day leaving only year
    filenm = yr "-Foo.log"  # concatenate rest of log filename
    print >> filenm         # append record to year file
  }
' input.txt

Use

Just modify the input filename and paste the foregoing at the command line in the directory with input.txt, or you can create an awk script from the content.

(Note: the NF < 2 { next } just skips lines with less than 2 fields [the empty ones in your example input], remove if there are no empty files, it doesn't hurt to keep it either)

(Also Note: this Appends to the output files each time you run it, you will want to rm [0-9]*-Foo.log between runs if you change things)

As a 1-liner:

$ awk 'NF < 2 { next } { yr = $1; sub (/-.*$/, "", yr); filenm = yr "-Foo.log"; print >> filenm }' input.txt

Resulting Files

-rw-r--r--. 1 david david   27 Jul  8 23:26 2022-Foo.log
-rw-r--r--. 1 david david   27 Jul  8 23:26 2023-Foo.log
-rw-r--r--. 1 david david   27 Jul  8 23:26 2024-Foo.log
-rw-r--r--. 1 david david   28 Jul  8 23:26 2025-Foo.log
-rw-r--r--. 1 david david   28 Jul  8 23:26 2026-Foo.log

Example file content

$ cat 2025-Foo.log
2025-12-19 18:00 Free: 3001

Q: Resolving Concurrency Bottlenecks in LangChain's RunnableParallel with ChromaDB PersistentClient A:

The existing answer's SQLite-lock diagnosis is correct, but there's a LangChain-specific wrinkle worth adding: PersistentClient has no async driver, so every call through it is synchronous no matter how you wire it into RunnableParallel.

Why this matters for "concurrency": if your retriever/tool wraps collection.query(...) and you invoke it via ainvoke/abatch, LangChain only gets real parallelism if that sync call is offloaded off the event loop thread. If a custom Runnable or retriever calls the sync Chroma API directly inside an async def without offloading it, you get serialized execution — no exceptions, just no actual concurrency, which can be misdiagnosed as a Chroma bug.

Fix — explicitly offload the sync Chroma call:

import asyncio
from functools import partial

def _sync_query(collection, query_texts, n_results):
    return collection.query(query_texts=query_texts, n_results=n_results)

async def aquery(collection, query_texts, n_results=5):
    # runs the blocking SQLite-backed call in a thread, off the event loop
    return await asyncio.to_thread(_sync_query, collection, query_texts, n_results)

This is exactly what LangChain's BaseRetriever._aget_relevant_documents does by default when a retriever only implements the sync method — worth confirming your custom retriever/tool isn't bypassing that fallback and calling the sync method inline inside an async context.

Combine both: cap concurrency with the semaphore from the existing answer and offload sync Chroma calls with asyncio.to_thread. For anything beyond light local dev/test load, Chroma's own guidance is the same as the existing answer: move to server mode (HttpClient/AsyncHttpClient against a Chroma server process), which removes SQLite file-locking from the equation entirely — see the Chroma client-server docs.

Note on busy_timeout: you might think of setting PRAGMA busy_timeout on SQLite to increase the wait window before "database is locked" errors. Problem is, PersistentClient doesn't expose its internal SQLite connection — and opening a separate sqlite3.connect() to set the pragma is a no-op (SQLite pragmas are per-connection state). This only works if you switch to server mode, where Chroma manages the connection lifecycle.

References:

  • Chroma client-server mode
  • LangChain BaseRetriever async fallback (_aget_relevant_documents)
  • Python asyncio.to_thread

Q: What is the best architecture for asynchronous jobs handling? A:

None of the above. The question doesn't describe an architecture anyway, it mentions the typical steps a client would take, then asks about reporting.

Architectural questions would be, do I use a library inside my service, do I use a separate job processing service, or do I use dedicated services like Airflow or Celery to orchestrate calls to APIs that actually execute the work? (OK that's overkill for simple apps and no throttling requirements)

The question confuses background processing with progress reporting and none of the mentioned options is really used to report progress. Instead, gRPC or WebSockets are used, depending on the type of client. SSE and worse polling are very expensive. They eat up server resources even though there's nothing new to report.

System.ThreadingChannels aren't relevant, they're a concurrency mechanism, the same as Go channels. Essentially, truly asynchronous queues. BUT SignalR, which can be used to report progress, uses them as an input source for streaming.

First of all, background processing .NET 10 already offers a mechanism for simple background processing, in the form of IHostedService and the basic implementation through BackgroundService. There's even a Worker service, but that doesn't refer to a Web API service, just hosting background services. The guide shows how you can create services that run on a simple schedule, or process queued messages. The queue is implemented using a Channel.

That only provides the hosting though, and provides no persistence, complex schedules, control, reporting etc. You'll have to write everything else you need yourself.

For more complex cases it's better to use libraries like Coravel, Hangfire, Quartz.NET. These libraries take care (more or less) of controlling jobs, persistence, handling dependent jobs. Some of them allow using multiple worker services to process a large number of jobs.

In all cases, you can put those services/libraries in your own application or run them as a separate web service.

Then, progress reporting. If the client is always connected, true push technologies like Websockets or gRPC server-side streaming are the cheapest and fastest.

gRPC is best for communication between services or generally non-web clients. It's a binary protocol based on messages that allows streaming in both ways. Browsers don't support all the transport mechanisms required for gRPC, so there's a gRPC-Web variant with reduced capabilities. ASP.NET Core supports that as well.

WebSockets is a lower-level mechanism that allows the server to call clients. It's used in a lot of SPA applications. Blazor Server uses it to send UI updates to the browser. You'll have to write a bit of code both on the client and server to handle them. It's supported by all browsers.

Finally, ASP.NET Core SignalR is a library that abstracts Websockets, SSEs and polling, to send messages to one or more clients. The primary mechanism is Websockets, with SSE as a fallback and worst-case, polling. It includes a JavaScript client that takes care of setting up communications with the server and handles disconnections and reconnections.

In one case I've used Hangfire in a Web API service that executes the jobs reports progress to web clients through ASP.NET Core SignalR. The WebUI issues requests to that API. The JS SignalR client receives the notifications.

Jobs are persisted to SQL Server, using Hangfire's built-in support. The client has a permanent SignalR connection to the SignalR hub and receives multiple messages, not just progress reports. The Hangfire docs show how to handle both polling and server-push through SignalR. You modify your job code to issue progress messages to an injected SignalR hub.

Coravel has an explicit mechanism to log or report events that can be used to do the same.
